To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
neocortical neurons can use their dendritic back-propagation of action potentials to predict future sensory input and learn to predict input sequences using a temporal difference learning mechanism.

the plasticity rule of neocortical recurrent synapses is governed, at least in part, by the temporal difference error between the predicted and the actual input and that this plasticity rule is capable of producing direction selectivity in the visual cortex.

neocortical circuits can learn to predict input sequences, that this learning rule can reproduce the temporal asymmetry of synaptic plasticity observed in neocortex, and that the resulting networks can develop direction selectivity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of recurrent excitation in cortical computation and the biophysical mechanisms that may underlie the learning and plasticity of recurrent synapses.
the role of recurrent neocortex in prediction and the development of direction selective cells.
the role of recurrent cortical synapses in learning to predict input sequences.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the neocortex is capable of learning to predict sequences of input stimuli, and this learning may underlie some of its functional properties.
the massive excitatory recurrent connectivity of the cortex can be used for prediction and that such a mechanism may contribute to the development of direction selectivity.
a temporally asymmetric learning rule for recurrent synapses can account for a number of physiological observations and is capable of generating direction selective responses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neocortex can learn predictive representations of input sequences by using temporally asymmetric plasticity of recurrent synapses.
recurrent neocortial circuits can learn to predict input sequences by a form of temporal sequence learning that is based on a temporally asymmetric plasticity rule.
the cortex can learn to predict input sequences and this may provide a basis for the development of direction selective neurons in the primary visual cortex.
The main takeaway from our work is that

recurrent neocortices can use the same synaptic learning rules as those found in the hippocampus to learn to predict sequences of inputs and that such learning can account for many of the observed response properties of neocortical neurons.
the neocortex may have a fundamental function of prediction, and that this function may be implemented by a temporally asymmetrical Hebbian learning process.
recurrent excitation in neocortex may be a consequence of its role in prediction and that this may be a general property of neocortical circuits.
